'''Paul Michael Grant''' (May 9, 1935&nbsp;– December 20, 2023) was an American/Irish physicist and science writer who was involved in discovering and elucidating the structure of [[yttrium barium copper oxide]] which was important as the first [[high temperature superconductor]] to exhibit superconductivity above the boiling point of nitrogen.<ref name="fizrev">{{Cite journal |last1=Grant |first1=P. M. |last2=Beyers |first2=R. B. |last3=Engler |first3=E. M. |last4=Lim |first4=G. |last5=Parkin |first5=S. S. P. |last6=Ramirez |first6=M. L. |last7=Lee |first7=V. Y. |last8=Nazzal |first8=A. |last9=Vazquez |first9=J. E. |last10=Savoy |first10=R. J. |year=1987 |title=Superconductivity above 90 K in the compound YBa2Cu3Ox: Structural, transport, and magnetic properties |url=https://journals.aps.org/prb/abstract/10.1103/PhysRevB.35.7242 |journal=Physical Review B |volume=35 |issue=13 |pages=7242–7244 |doi=10.1103/PhysRevB.35.7242 |pmid=9941013|url-access=subscription }}</ref><ref>[https://web.archive.org/web/20190904192139/https://pdfs.semanticscholar.org/5ca8/13204ddef29232f2006ace2f06bdc0f87a18.pdf A. Malozemoff et al., "Superconductivity at IBM - a Centennial Review: Part II – Materials and Physics", IEEE/CSC & ESAS European Superconductivity News Forum, No. 20, July 2012]</ref> He was a co-author of IBM's US patent application covering their preparation.<ref name=patent>[http://brevets-patents.ic.gc.ca/opic-cipo/cpd/eng/patent/1341623/summary.html Canadian Patent CA1341623C refers to US provisional patent application US2465387A filed 1987-03-11]</ref><ref name=bio>[http://www.w2agz.com/About_PMG.htm W2AGZ Paul Grant biography]</ref><ref name=Clarkson>[https://cuonline.clarkson.edu/s/1680/index.aspx?sid=1680&gid=2&pgid=252&cid=2044&ecid=2044&crid=0&calpgid=528&calcid=1282 Clarkson University Biography: Paul Grant]</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |url=https://www.researchgate.net/publication/11952718 |doi=10.1038/35079212 |title=Rehearsals for prime time |year=2001 |last1=Grant |first1=Paul |journal=Nature |volume=411 |issue=6837 |pages=532–533 |pmid=11385548 |s2cid=4423073 }}</ref>

== Career ==
Grant joined IBM [[Poughkeepsie]], NY in 1953 working as a technician on the [[Semi-Automatic Ground Environment|SAGE]] computer defense system.<ref>[https://www.computerhistory.org/revolution/real-time-computing/6/120 Computer History Museum: SAGE Defense System]</ref> He was able to take advantage of IBM's educational leave-of-absence program to obtain a BS degree from Clarkson and a Ph.D. from Harvard.<ref>[http://w2agz.com/Library/IBM%20Personal%20History/IBM%20Kingston%20News%2025%20May%201960.pdf IBM Kingston News, Vol. 5, No. 21, May 25, 1960]</ref>

In 1957, he filed a patent<ref>[https://patents.google.com/patent/US3016507A/en?oq=3016507 US Patent 3016507, "Thin film magneto resistance device" 1962-01-09]</ref> that is cited as a precursor to the [[magnetoresistive]] head used universally in [[magnetic recording]]. In 1965, he moved to [[IBM Research – Almaden]]. At IBM, Grant was among the team researching superconductivity in the material [[Yttrium Barium Copper Oxide]] (YBCO) and found it to exhibit superconductivity at temperatures as high as 90 K.<ref name="fizrev" /> This patent application provided some of first evidence that superconductivity could be supported at temperatures above the boiling point of [[nitrogen]], a common [[cryogenic]] refrigerant.

In 1987–88, with guidance from Grant, his 8th-grade daughter, Heidi, and then subsequently a science class at [[Gilroy High School]], were able to show the relative ease with which high temperature superconductors could be fabricated and demonstrated.<ref name="newscientist" /><ref>[https://www.nytimes.com/1988/01/12/science/superconductivity-moves-from-the-laboratory-to-the-classroom.html M. Browne, "Superconductivity Moves From the Laboratory to the Classroom" NY Times, Jan. 12, 1988]</ref><ref>[https://www.ibm.com/blogs/research/2011/06/ibm100-remembering-1987-nobel-prize-for-physics/ IBM Research Blog, June 2011]</ref>

Also in 1987, Grant became the manager of the group at IBM devoted to research on exotic new materials, including superconductors. When high-Tc cuprate superconductors were discovered at IBM Zurich that same year, Grant became the driving force behind the work at IBM Research - Almaden in this hot new area. IBM Almaden made many important discoveries related to these cuprate superconductors, with Grant involved on most of them.

From 1990 to 1993, Grant was a "visiting faculty researcher" at the Instituto de Investigationes Materiales (IIM), [[National Autonomous University of Mexico]] (UNAM), where he carried out numerical studies on the properties of rare earth copper oxides. From 1993 to 2004, he was a Science [[Fellow]] with the [[Electric Power Research Institute]] (EPRI).

In 2004, Grant started his own consulting business<ref name="website" /><ref name="bio" /> and became an assiduous advocate for commercial applications of superconductivity.<ref>[https://physicsworld.com/a/where-next-for-superconductivity/ Physics World video, "Where next for superconductivity", 6th Apr. 2011]</ref><ref>[http://w2agz.com/PMG%20SuperGrid%20Home.htm P. Grant, "The Energy Supergrid"]</ref> He was a popular science writer<ref name="newscientist">[https://books.google.com/books?id=Qe_hJ8qZb7oC P. Grant, "Do-it-yourself superconductors", New Scientist, pp. 36-38 30 July 1987 ]</ref><ref>[https://physiology.med.cornell.edu/faculty/nirenberg/lab/pel/environment/hydrogen_nature03.pdf P. Grant, "Hydrogen lifts off — with a heavy load", Nature Vol. 424, 10 July 2003]</ref><ref>{{cite journal | url=https://www.nature.com/articles/420743a?proof=true | doi=10.1038/420743a | title=London calling | year=2002 | last1=Grant | first1=Paul M. | journal=Nature | volume=420 | issue=6917 | pages=743–744 | s2cid=38765396 | url-access=subscription }}</ref><ref>[https://phe.rockefeller.edu/docs/SA_Supergrid.pdf P. Grant, C. Starr, T. Overbye, "A power grid for the hydrogen economy", Scientific American, pp. 77-83, July 2006]</ref> and a prolific author of scientific papers and patents,<ref>[https://scholar.google.com/citations?user=1h7W-xkAAAAJ&hl=en&oi=sra Google Citations: Paul Grant]</ref><ref>[http://w2agz.com/Publications/Patent%20Publications/09%20(1999)123%20Complete.zip Paul Grant publications and patents]</ref> and a member of the Storage Interest Group<ref>[https://www.computerhistory.org/groups/storagesig/ Storage Interest Group, Computer History Museum, Mountain View, California]</ref> at the [[Computer History Museum]]. From 2005 to 2008, he was a visiting scholar in applied physics at [[Stanford University]].

==Patent dispute ==
In 2000, a patent dispute over the invention of YBCO (see above) dating back to March 1987 was finally resolved.  The dispute was between IBM's Almaden Research Center, the US Naval Research Laboratory, the University of Houston, and Bell Labs.  Ultimately, [[Bell Labs]]. prevailed and was granted the US patent based on priority date (date of invention rather than the current criterion of date of filing).<ref>[https://physicstoday.scitation.org/doi/pdf/10.1063/1.883038 Tony Feder, "Bell Labs Wins Long-Running Patent Battle over High-Tc Superconductor", Physics Today 53, 4, 56 (2000)]</ref><ref>{{cite journal | doi=10.1038/35003008 | title=Bell Labs win superconductivity patent | year=2000 | last1=MacIlwain | first1=Colin | journal=Nature | volume=403 | issue=6766 | pages=121–122 | pmid=10646568 | s2cid=1120705 | doi-access=free }}</ref>

==Recognition and awards ==
Grant became a Senior [[Fellow of the American Physical Society]] in 1998 "For contributions to the fields of organic conductors and high temperature superconductivity".<ref>[https://www.aps.org/programs/honors/fellowships/archive-all.cfm APS Fellow Archive]</ref> He became a [[Fellow of the Institute of Physics]], United Kingdom, in Nov 2004.

In 2013, Grant was chosen as [[American Physical Society]] Distinguished Lecturer on the Applications of Physics.<ref>[https://www.aps.org/units/fiap/newsletters/201311/lectureship.cfm APS Newsletter Fall 2013 "Paul Grant chosen as the 2014 Distinguished Lecturer"]</ref>

Grant was also one of Clarkson University's "Notable Knights".<ref>[https://cuonline.clarkson.edu/s/1680/index.aspx?sid=1680&gid=2&pgid=528 Clarkson University Notable Knights]</ref>

== Science writing ==
Grant was a prolific science writer, for both professional and popular audiences.  He wrote multiple articles and ''News and Views'' commentaries on a range of topics for the journal ''[[Nature (journal)|Nature]]''.

== Final years ==
In 2021, Grant retired to [[Ajijic]], Mexico with his wife Maru Grant. He died on December 20, 2023.
